topics.title: Technical skills checklist
topics.path: Unit 1: Developing Skills in Data Analysis
topics.html:
Technical Skills Checklist

This checklist summarizes the core technical skills developed throughout the course. Skills are grouped by software, with a continuous numbered list in each section. Use it to review your progress and identify skills that may require additional practice.


Checklist update — 12 October 2026: Additional skills are shown in blue and marked Added. These were not included in the original checklist.

  • Excel and Power Query
  • QGIS
  • Positron and R

Excel

  1. I can open an Excel workbook and identify its worksheets, tables, variables, and observations.
  2. I can import a CSV file into Excel.
  3. I can open and navigate the Power Query Editor.
  4. I can insert rows and columns when restructuring a worksheet.
  5. I can format a dataset as an Excel table.
  6. I can assign appropriate number, text, date, and time formats to columns.
  7. I can select and inspect columns in Power Query.
  8. I can identify null values, errors, unexpected values, and formatting problems.
  9. I can remove or correct null and error values using Power Query.
  10. I can filter data using Power Query.
  11. I can select, retain, remove, and reorder columns appropriately.
  12. I can parse data and then extract the year and month from a date variable.
  13. I can pivot and unpivot data using Power Query.
  14. I can explain understand the difference between wide and long data formats.
  15. I can create a PivotTable from an Excel dataset.
  16. I can organize PivotTable rows and columns and calculate sums, averages, and counts.
  17. I can filter a PivotTable.
  18. I can extract the underlying records represented by a summarized PivotTable value.
  19. I can create a PivotChart as an initial visualization of summarized data.
  20. I can use PivotTable and PivotChart field controls to explore different subsets of the data.
  21. I can perform calculations across worksheets using existing variables (e.g., count if).
  22. I can calculate sums, averages, minimums, and maximums.
  23. I can use IFS or nested IF statements to represent several possible conditions.
  24. Added: I can use UNIQUE() to create a list of distinct values from a column.
  25. I can combine conditions using logical operators such as AND and OR.
  26. I can use the FILTER function to return a subset of a dataset. 
  27. I can use Power Query to merge two datasets using a shared field.
  28. I can expand selected columns from a merged dataset.
  29. I can select a chart type that is appropriate for the variables and analytical question.
  30. I can use field buttons to change the data displayed in a PivotChart.
  31. I can remove field buttons when preparing a chart for presentation.
  32. I can sort categories into an informative order.

QGIS

  1. I can load a CSV file into QGIS.
  2. I can load an ESRI Shapefile into QGIS.
  3. I can load a raster dataset into QGIS.
  4. I can add a basemap to a QGIS project.
  5. I can open and explore a layer’s attribute table.
  6. I can identify a layer’s coordinate reference system and reproject a vector layer when necessary.
  7. I can identify a raster layer’s coordinate reference system and reproject it when necessary.
  8. I can change a field’s data type when it has been imported incorrectly using the Field Calculator.
  9. I can identify and repair invalid vector geometries using Fix Geometries. 
  10. I can create a basic exploratory map to inspect the distribution of spatial data.
  11. I can filter a spatial layer using one attribute condition.
  12. I can filter a spatial layer using multiple conditions and operators such as IN.
  13. I can distinguish between temporarily filtering features and permanently creating a new filtered dataset.
  14. I can export layers as a new Shapefile, CSV file or GeoPackage.
  15. I can use the Field Calculator to create a new attribute from existing fields.
  16. I can use conditional expressions in the Field Calculator to classify spatial features.
  17. I can calculate geometry attributes such as area, length, or coordinates.
  18. I can use the Raster Calculator to create a new raster from one or more input layers.
  19. Added: I can use Raster Calculator to classify raster cells using a cutoff value
  20. I can create a new vector layer with an appropriate geometry type and coordinate reference system.
  21. I can create, edit and save polygon features. 
  22. Added: I can export selected spatial attributes to their own Shapefile.
  23. I can join a non-spatial table to a spatial layer using a shared attribute using Join. 
  24. I can use Join Attributes by Nearest to add attributes from other vector layers. 
  25. I can measure distances between spatial features.
  26. I can use Join Attributes by Location to connect features that intersect or occur within one another.
  27. I can count the number of points contained within polygons.
  28. Added: I can use Clip to retain the parts of a spatial layer that fall within a study-area boundary.
  29. I can create buffers around spatial features using Buffer.
  30. I can sample raster values at point locations using Sample Raster Values.
  31. I can summarize raster categories within polygons using a zonal histogram.
  32. I can change the appearance of vector features including point shapes.
  33. I can symbolize categorical  and quantitative data using categorized/graduated symbols or colour gradients.
  34. I can select an appropriate classification method (e.g., Equal Intervals) and number of classes.
  35. I can display raster values using an appropriate pseudocolour scheme.
  36. I can use Overlap Analysis to identify places where vector layers overlap.
  37. I can initiate a QGIS print layout.
  38. I can add and position a map within a print layout.
  39. I can add a north arrow and a appropriate scale bar.
  40. I can add and format a legend including removing, renaming, reordering, and grouping legend items.
  41. I can add a frame and coordinate system to a map. 
  42. I can export a finished map at an appropriate size and resolution.

Positron and R

  1. I can install R packages using install.packages() and load them using library().
  2. I can check my working directory using getwd() and work from the appropriate data folder.
  3. I can load a CSV file using read_csv() and assign the result to an object using <-.
  4. I can clean imported column names using clean_names() from the janitor package.
  5. I can inspect the first rows of a dataset using head().
  6. I can inspect column names, data types, and example values using names() and glimpse().
  7. I can identify the distinct values in a variable using unique() and access a column using $.
  8. I can use the pipe operators |> and %>% to connect data-processing steps.
  9. I can select, remove, and reorder columns using select().
  10. I can select or exclude columns by name or position and use backticks around column names containing spaces.
  11. I can rename variables using rename().
  12. I can filter observations using one or more conditions with filter().
  13. I can use %in% to retain or exclude several categories.
  14. I can use %in% with a column from another dataset to retain selected stations or groups.
  15. I can filter using ==, !=, >, and >=, and combine or reverse conditions using & and !.
  16. I can use complete.cases() to exclude missing values from selected variables.
  17. I can convert values to numeric using as.numeric().
  18. I can convert a variable to text using as.character().
  19. I can parse date-time strings using ymd_hm() and dates using mdy().
  20. I can extract labelled months using month(..., label = TRUE).
  21. I can control category order using factor(..., levels = ...).
  22. I can create or modify variables using mutate().
  23. I can use ifelse() to classify observations or replace a specified value with NA.
  24. I can group observations by one or more variables using group_by().
  25. I can calculate grouped summaries using summarize().
  26. I can calculate grouped totals, maxima, and means using sum(), max(), and mean().
  27. I can use na.rm = TRUE to omit missing values from summary calculations.
  28. I can count records within groups using n() inside summarize().
  29. I can count distinct values using n_distinct()
  30. I can sort summary values using arrange() and retain the first few rows using head().
  31. I can reshape data from wide to long using pivot_longer().
  32. I can reshape data from long to wide using pivot_wider().
  33. I can write a transformed dataset to a CSV file using write_csv().
  34. I can construct a plot using ggplot() and map variables to position, colour, fill, and group using aes().
  35. I can create column charts using geom_col().
  36. I can create scatterplots using geom_point().
  37. I can create boxplots using geom_boxplot().
  38. I can create line graphs using geom_line() to connect observations across categorical months.
  39. I can plot a date-time variable on an axis to explore change through time.
  40. I can create histograms using geom_histogram().
  41. I can create stacked column charts by mapping categories to fill in geom_col().
  42. I can create a heatmap using geom_tile() and map a summarized value to tile fill.
  43. I can add numeric values or descriptive labels using geom_text().
  44. I can round numeric labels using round() and adjust text size and position using size, hjust, and vjust.
  45. I can use a separate dataset in a plot layer to highlight or label selected observations.
  46. I can distinguish between mapping colour inside aes() and assigning a fixed colour outside it.
  47. I can manually set mapped line and point colours using scale_colour_manual().
  48. I can control point transparency using alpha, point size using size.
  49. I can add a fitted trend using geom_smooth() and specify a straight-line fit using method = "lm".
  50. I can add informative titles, subtitles, axis labels, and legend titles using labs().
  51. I can change the overall appearance of a plot using theme_bw() or theme_classic().
  52. I can customize titles, subtitles, axis titles, axis text, and legend text using theme() and element_text().
  53. I can rotate axis labels and adjust their alignment to improve readability.
  54. I can move a legend using legend.position or hide it using legend.position = "none".
  55. I can reorder categories by a summary value using reorder(), including changing the sort direction.
  56. I can divide a visualization into panels using facet_wrap().
  57. I can flip the axes of a plot using coord_flip().
  58. I can export a PNG using ggsave() and specify its width, height, and units.
  59. I can fit a simple linear regression using lm() with a formula such as y ~ x.
  60. I can inspect a fitted model using summary() and identify the estimated slope and its p-value.
  61. I can interpret a regression result in relation to the question being investigated.
  62. I can compare a response between groups using a section predictor in a linear model.
  63. I can fit a model with multiple predictors using an additive formula such as y ~ section + distance.
  64. I can include an interaction using a formula such as y ~ section * distance and distinguish it from an additive model.
  65. Added: I can combine datasets containing the same variables using bind_rows().
  66. Added: I can add information from another dataset using left_join() and explain which records it retains.
  67. Added: I can retain records that have a match in another dataset using semi_join().
  68. Added: I can identify records without a match in another dataset using anti_join().
  69. Added: I can specify matching columns using join_by(), including columns with different names in the two datasets.
  70. Added: I can retain unique records using distinct() and preserve other columns using .keep_all = TRUE.

topics.html:
Getting Started with Course Software

In our course, we will be using a broad range of software to ensure that you are competent and confident with accessing and using data. Do not worry if you have never worked in any of these programs, the course is designed to ensure that we start from scratch. If you have used these programs before, you may feel free to skip over videos where you have already mastered the skills.  I've have linked a few helpful introductory videos here to help you get acquantied (or reaquainted) with these software tools. 

Excel 

All of you have access to Microsoft Excel through your Office 365 on your Western accounts. For our class, you need to download the desktop application. You can log into your account with your Western credentials https://m365.cloud.microsoft/apps and then click on “Install apps” in the top right corner to install Excel on your desktop (shown in the screenshot below). 

I'm sure many of you are already familiar with Excel; however, if you need a bit of an introduction to fundamentals of how Excel works, can you view the video below from Kevin Stratvert :

https://youtu.be/Ai0MV7twEBE?si=eqUe3eA4z3LR2SPx

QGIS

QGIS is an open-source geographic information systems program (GIS). This program is compatible with both Macs and PCs. You can download QGIS from here - https://qgis.org/

Please be aware that if you are a Mac user, you will need to ensure that your operating system (OS) is updated to the latest version and you may need to approve the app download in your security settings.  You can download the most updated version for Mac here, which should be sufficient for our purposes.  

For everyone, I would recommend download the Long Term Release (LTR) version of QGIS. 

Statistics Canada has developed an introductory video on QGIS, which you can access below to gain a better understanding of why we will be analysing spatial data with QGIS. 

  • What is GIS, and why use QGIS? 

Positron and R

Many of you may already have some experience using R and the open-source code editor RStudio. Posit, the company behind RStudio, has recently released a new code editor called Positron.

Positron builds on many of the strengths of RStudio while offering additional tools for working with and exploring data. I think its workflow will not only make data analysis more intuitive, but also help you develop stronger skills in R as you work through the course.

You can download Positron here - https://positron.posit.co/download.html

  • A quick tour of Positron
    • This is a very quick introduction to the layout of Positron, which may look a bit familiar if you have used RStudio in your undergraduate courses. We will be going over the set-up and layout of Positron in more depth through the class material. 

R Language

Positron will be your code editor, but you still need to download R for your computer here (https://cran.r-project.org/.  You will want to download the base version of R for your operating system (current version is 4.6.1). Once you have that version downloaded, it will automatically be detected by Positron. 

R is an object-oriented programming language that is extremely popular for data analysis. We will be using R, and particularly a group of packages called The Tidyverse,  extensively for data analysis in the course. Before the course begins, you should watch the following video, but feel free to skip sections if you are already comfortable with those skills. 

  • R programming in one hour - a crash course for beginners
    • Note, this is a fairly quick (he literally speaks quite quickly) to the overall R language. We are going to be going over all of the things covered in this video, so you don't need to walk away from this video with a deep understanding of R,  but it is an excellent introduction to many of the functions and packages (e.g., ggplot2) that we are going to be using. 

Python

Depending upon our progress in the course, we are planning to explore the use of Python for large-scale geospatial analysis. 
I will revisit this as the course progresses and add additional instructions here as needed, but for now, there is no further action to be taken.

topics.html:
The National Pollutant Release Inventory

For most of our data analysis training, we will use the National Pollutant Release Inventory (NPRI) as our foundational dataset. The NPRI is Canada's publicly accessible inventory of pollutant releases, disposals, and transfers reported annually by industrial and commercial facilities across the country. Working with a common dataset has two main advantages for us:

  1. By working with a common dataset throughout the term, we can focus on building core analytical skills such as data cleaning, management, visualization, exploration, and interpretation without needing to learn a new dataset for every topic area. This allows us to progressively build our technical skills while simultaneously developing a deeper understanding of the data, its structure, and its limitations.
  2. Later in the term, the NPRI dataset will form the foundation of your NPRI group project, where you will apply the methods and tools learned throughout the course to investigate an environmental question of interest. By working with the dataset throughout the term, you will be better prepared to conduct meaningful analyses, identify trends and patterns, and communicate evidence-based insights through your final project.

Before the first class, please review the following two videos:

  • The National Pollutant Release Inventory (NPRI)
  • Instructional videos: National Pollutant Release Inventory - Canada.ca (How to use Excel tabular data)

In addition, it will be helpful for you to see the spatial data that is attached to the NPRI. Quickly explore the NPRI map linked below.

  • National Pollutant Release Inventory Map - Canada.ca

You can download the NPRI datasets you need here:

 NPRI data.zip

You must download the folder and unzip it if you are on a Windows machine (right click, Extract All).

Topic 1: Loading, Cleaning and Exploring Data

The first step in data exploration is the process of loading, cleaning and exploring data. Each of the software packages we use has a different mechanism for this and our goal for this Topic is to understand how to load and complete basic manipulations with our datasets. 

Learning objectives

In this lesson, we'll focus on developing the basic essential skills for importing,  manipulating and visualizing your data across Excel, R and QGIS. 

  • Locate and successfully import datasets into Excel, R (via Positron), and QGIS using correct file formats and import procedures.
  • Apply appropriate formatting techniques to ensure data is clean, consistent, and ready for analysis, including handling dates and times, and setting up data for visualization in each platform
  • Aggregate and plot data within Excel using Pivot Tables and Charts
  • Create simple visual representations of data in Excel and R, as well as maps in QGIS that support initial data exploration 

 

Video resources

Excel 

  • Excel - Intro to Excel
    • This video provides a brief (re) introduction to Excel and goes over some of the functionality we will be using. It also takes you through the steps to add the Data Analysis ToolPak in Excel. 
  • Excel - Loading data into Excel
    • A short video on how to open files within Excel and how to import data into Table format. 
  • Excel - Basic filtering
    • Simple filtering using the Power Query Editor 
  • Excel - Pivot tables and charts
    • Introduction to aggregating and summarizing data in Pivot tables and charts.

QGIS

Below, I've included several videos from the Statistics Canada QGIS demo. The Statistics Canada videos move quite quickly and use a range of datasets, which unfortunately they do not provide openly. You do not  need to follow along with their datasets in the videos, but they do a good job of exposing you to the tool and techniques that allow you to access and use data within QGIS. For the course videos (e.g., QGIS - Adding a delimited text layer), you can download the datasets and work along on your computer The NPRI Dataset.

* When you click on the Statistics Canada links, you need to click "Go to Publication" before it will direct you to the video. 

  • QGIS - Introduction to QGIS
    • Tour of QGIS layout and features
  • QGIS - CRS
    • Discussion of the Coordinate Reference System and how to modify it in QGIS
  • QGIS - Base maps
    • Introduction to the QuickMapServices plugin for QGIS
  • Types of Spatial Data (Statistics Canada)
    • A nice introduction to different types of spatial data you can use with QGIS
  • Loading and ordering spatial data in QGIS (Statistics Canada)
    • Introduction to loading vector data into the Layers panel
  • QGIS - Adding a shapefile
    • Alternative way of loading in shapefiles quickly by dragging and dropping into the browser directly
  • QGIS - Adding a delimited text layer
    • An important skill that allows you to add non-spatial CSVs with coordinate data to QGIS (you'll be doing this a lot!)
  • Interacting with the Map Canvas (Statistics Canada)
    • A nice tour through how you can interact with loaded spatial data in the map canvas
  • Vector Data - Exploring the Attribute Table and Layer Properties Box (Statistics Canada)
    • Good introductory video into the Attribute Table and altering layer properties. 
  • QGIS - Basic filter in QGIS
    • Simple Attribute Table filtering 
  • Visualizing Vector Data (Statistics Canada)
    • This video is a very rapid overview of all the different ways you can change vector symbology, we'll be trying a lot of these out ourselves but this serves as a general intro.

Positron

I've included a short introduction to Positron below. I will be adding a few more videos here before the start of class to go through loading data and visualization.  

  • Positron - Introduction and package installation
    • Walkthrough of Positron and package installation in R

topics.html:
Topic 2: Transforming and wrangling data

In this topic, we will focus primarily on the task of reorganizing our datasets to prepare them for exploratory data analysis. We are going to cover 

Excel

  • Excel - Data and variable types
    • This video goes through loading data into Power Query and then checking for data type errors
  • Excel - Splitting columns
    • Here, we explore how we can separate data out from a single column to create additional variables
  • Excel - Selecting and removing columns and rows
    • Quick introduction to removing columns and rows as well as removing blanks and duplicates
  • Excel - Pivoting columns
    • This covers the very useful step of pivoting and unpivoting data into wide and long format

For the following videos, please download and import OBIS - North Atlantic Right Whale reduced.csv

  • Excel - Extracting date information
  • Excel - Cleaning up date data

QGIS

In these videos, we'll look at how raster data can be added to QGIS and how we can manipulate it. We'll also explore some additional options to filter vector data. 

For the videos below that involve raster import, I've sourced both raster and ESRI Rest Servers for Marine Invasive Species (NPRI doesn't have a good range of raster files). Download the following raster files for the green shore crab and the sea vase:

    • Carcinus maenas.tif
    • Ciona intestinalis.tif
  • QGIS - Raster import
    • This video reviews how raster data can be imported into QGIS and how we can alter the symbology for visualization
  • QGIS - Raster calculator

Topic 5: Connecting Data - Joins, merges, and spatial relationships

In this topic, we focus on connecting datasets using shared attributes and spatial relationships. You will learn how to merge tables in Excel using Power Query, combine and bind datasets in R, and use QGIS to connect spatial information across vector and raster layers.  The majority of work for this topic will be in QGIS. You need to download the following data folder:

  • Topic 5.zip

Open datasets

  • Provincial Water Quality Monitoring Network (PWQMN)
    The PWQMN is an Ontario-wide monitoring program that collects long-term water-quality data from rivers and streams. The dataset includes monitoring-station locations and measurements of parameters such as nutrients, metals, and chloride, making it useful for exploring how environmental measurements can be linked to spatial sampling locations.
  • Agricultural Resource Inventory (ARI)
    The Agricultural Resource Inventory is a historical spatial dataset describing agricultural land use systems in southern Ontario. It classifies agricultural areas based on crop patterns and land use, providing a useful spatial layer for examining the agricultural character of the landscape. 

Excel 

  • Excel - Merging data (4:33)
    • Here, we review how you can use the Power Query tool to merge data from two separate tables

QGIS

For these videos, we'll be exploring the buckthorn data we collected on Monday. 

  • QGIS - Creating a new layer (5:04)
    • How to create a new vector layer (polygon) manually within QGIS
  • QGIS - Reprojecting a vector layer (4:05)
    • Reprojecting layers to new CRS (e.g., switching to units measured in metres)
  • QGIS - Join attributes by nearest (11:04)
    • Measuring distances between two vector layers using join attributes by nearest
  • QGIS - Sample raster values (5:23)
    • Attach raster values to vector data by pulling pixel data where vectors points overlap
  • QGIS - Exporting attribute table to CSV (3:00)
    • Exporting attributes tables to a CSV

For these videos, we are going to look at the Provincial Water Quality Monitoring Network. 

  • QGIS - Spatial joins  (8:36)
    • This video introduces the idea of joining a spatial dataset (e.g., with longitude and latitude) with a dataset that has no spatial information
  • QGIS - Changing column types (1:58)
    • In cases where data types are incorrect (e.g., text when it should be a number) you can change the data type within the field calculator
  • QGIS - Join attributes by location (3:41)
    • This tool allows the user to take two vector layers (e.g., a point and polygon layer) and pull information from one to another based on the location
  • QGIS - Buffer creation and zonal histograms (9:39)
    • In this video, we explore how to make buffers around vector features and then subsequently, how we can use zonal histograms to characterise an underlying raster layer

Pollution Pathways: Tracking Canada’s Environmental Releases

National Pollutant Release Inventory

This week, we are being visited by a representative from the National Pollutant Release Inventory team. This topic's readings are all about becoming more familiar with the NPRI and how they monitor and publicly share data on pollutants. 

1. Using and interpreting data from the National Pollutant Release Inventory - Canada.ca
Summary: NPRI has provided a great range of resources for helping to understand, access, and interpret their data. The linked page has a number of "tabs" that I would like you to move through to deepen your understanding of the NPRI data. 

Guidance:  I would like you to work through each of the tabbed sections:
(1) About Us - Entire section with focus on main infographic and Evolution of the NPRI over time
(2) Using our Data - Entire section and take good note of some of the common analysis mistakes, you can skim quickly through the specific substances listed under Avoid double or triple counting 
(3) Interpreting our Data - Read entire section casually, but you can skip the Waste rock components. Special focus on Understanding changes
(4) Our Method - Quickly skim this section

2.  National Pollutant Release Inventory Dashboard - Canada.ca 

Summary: More and more organizations are making use of PowerBI dashboards and digital interfaces to communicate their findings to the public. This is a really great example of a PowerBI dashboard created by ECCC to demonstrate the powerful insights that can be gained from the NPRI dataset.

Guidance:  I would recommend first taking the dashboard to full screen (). Then explore the range of interactivity throughout the dashboard.

  • Explore the NPRI data -> Explore data for a community ->  Select London
    • Compare 2024 to 2014, are there any major differences in emitters? 
    • Go back and select your home city or somewhere outside of London if you are from here. What types of emissions are common?  How many emitters are in your region?
  • Explore the NPRI data -> Explore one year of NPRI data 
    • Click on Conventional Oil and Gas Extraction, where are the majority of those facilities located in the updated map? 
    • Use the interactive pie chart to determine which sector leads in releases to air. 
    • Try filtering substances to 1a, what is the leading release in this category? 
    • Reset the dashboard to "Show All Data"  and then determine which sector has the highest emissions of particulate matter and then ammonia. 
    • What is the leading release of the metals industry and where are producers concentrated?
  • Move back to the homepage of the dashboard and select, Drill into data by location, sector, substance
    • Select Ontario, Pulp and Paper Mills, and Paper (except newsprint) Mills
    • How has this sector's emissions changed over time?
  • Go back to homepage and selection Search for facility-level data
    • Search for 3M Canada Company and select the London facility. 
    • Select the Release and Transfer button
    • What are the two main releases to air in 2018? 

3. NPRI data highlights 2023

Summary: The highlights report provides a high-level overview of pollutant releases, with the vast majority being released to the air.  

Guidance: Review the following sections:

  • 2024 Data at a Glance
  • 'Regional Overview' for each area, with specific attention to the top sectors and pollutants.

topics.html:
Beneath the Surface: Measuring Animal Abundance in the Ocean

The North Atlantic right whale, an iconic giant of Canada's Bay of Fundy, teeters on the brink of extinction (IUCN 2020). Once abundant, their numbers have dwindled to a few hundred due to human activities. Entanglement in fishing gear and ship strikes pose the most significant threats to their population stability. 

This class will introduce the course philosophy, structure, and layout. We will begin to practice and develop our technical skills in data manipulation, management, and visualization using a range of software packages. The class will explore the goals and objectives of conservation biology, with a particular focus on the challenges of marine conservation for highly migratory species.

Learning Objectives

In this lesson, we'll focus on developing the basic essential skills for importing,  manipulating and visualizing your data across Excel, R and QGIS. 

  • Locate and successfully import datasets into Excel, R, and QGIS using correct file formats and import procedures.
  • Apply appropriate formatting techniques to ensure data is clean, consistent, and ready for analysis, including handling dates and times, and setting up data for visualization in each platform
  • Aggregate and plot data within Excel using Pivot Tables and Charts
  • Create simple visual representations of data in R and maps in QGIS that support initial data exploration 

Lesson outline

  1. Practice! (20 minutes)
  2. Introduction to course structure and layout  (35 mins)

  4. Positron lesson (55 minutes)
  5. BREAK

Animals on the Move: Tracking Animal Movement Across Seascapes

Understanding the causes of animal movement can help us better predict when and where animals will encounter threats and risks. However, animal movement is complex, often driven by a multitude of internal and external factors, and particularly challenging to study in marine environments.

In this lesson, we will explore some of the most common technologies used to track animals across landscapes and seascapes, including satellite tags, acoustic arrays, and biologgers. We'll focus on basking sharks as a model species to examine how tracking data can reveal migratory pathways, habitat preferences, and risk exposure in ocean ecosystems. 

Environmental Analysis Learning Objectives

  • Apply filtering techniques across Excel, R, and QGIS to extract relevant subsets of data for analysis

  • Import, process, and manipulate raster and vector datasets in QGIS

topics.html:
Marine Sportfish Tagging Programme

Background

Citizen science is a growing source of reliable data for many groups of species. Portals include:

  • https://ebird.org/home
  • https://www.inaturalist.org/

In this case study, we're going to look at The Marine Sportfish Tagging Programme established by Inland Fisheries Ireland. Here is a quick overview of the data:

  • Established in 1970 to promote catch-and-release of elasmobranchs (sharks, skates, rays) at a time when most catches were kept.
  • One of the longest-running tagging programmes of its kind worldwide.
  • Over 50 years, more than 40,000 fish tagged and over 3,000 recaptures recorded.
  • Data has revealed migration patterns, local extinctions (e.g., angelshark), and seasonal site fidelity in species like juvenile porbeagle.
  • Citizen science encouraged — anglers can report tagged fish 

The Data

    You can find the dataset here.
    • Irish_Marine_Sports_Fish_Tagging_Programme_Dataset_Full.csv

    Case Study Objectives

    The following are some open-ended objectives I want you and your team to work on. 

    You are preparing a short briefing for program managers at Inland Fisheries Ireland on the citizen-science tagging program. Use the dataset to show how the program has developed over time, who and what is contributing to the records, and any important temporal or species-level patterns you identify.

    Use well-chosen visualizations and a concise narrative to highlight the most important findings. Conclude by considering what your results might mean for the future of the program, including potential priorities for monitoring, outreach, or resourcing.

Invasive Species Monitoring

Invasive species are one of the leading causes of biodiversity loss globally. Many environmental non-governmental organizations, municipalities, and provincial/federal governments spend significant time and financial resources on preventing or removing invasive species from the ecosystem. For our applied case study today, we will be running our own invasive species survey for buckthorn to determine focus areas for removal later in the semester.  As part of this process, we will focus on real data collection and processing. 

Environmental Analysis Learning Objectives

  • Be familiar with standard ecological sampling techniques
  • Accurately collect and digitize data for invasive species monitoring
  • Conduct exploratory data analysis to determine areas to target areas of high priority for invasive species removal

Troubled Waters: 
A History of Pollution in Canadian Waterways

Living in Southwestern Ontario, we are directly connected to the Laurentian Great Lakes, one of the largest freshwater systems on the planet. These lakes provide drinking water to London, recreation, transportation, and fisheries, but they also face persistent threats from pollution and environmental change. In this lesson, we will examine some of the most important pollutants affecting our local freshwater systems.  One area of focus will be eutrophication and the its primary causes (agriculture, wastewater, etc.) and consequences (e.g., harmful algal blooms). We will also take a historical look back at acid rain, once a major driver of ecological damage across Ontario, to understand its causes, impacts, and how coordinated policy efforts helped bring the problem under control. 

    Environmental Analysis Learning Objectives

    • Perform data joins to combine datasets from multiple sources, including attribute joins, spatial joins, and joins by location.
    • Integrate and merge data in Excel, R, and QGIS to support more complex analyses.
    • Extract and link spatial information by sampling raster and vector values and joining them to vector datasets for further analysis.

    Lesson outline

    1. Pre-class work review (1 hour)
    2. Case study #5: Exploring sulfate concentrations and the Provincial Water Quality Monitoring Network (2 hours)
    3. Introduction to the NPRI assignment (30 minutes)

topics.path: Unit 1 Classes: Core Technical Skills > Class 5 - Troubled Waters: A History of Pollution in Canadian Waterways
topics.html:
Troubled Waters: 
A History of Pollution in Canadian Waterways

Sulphate wet deposition

In this section, you will explore the distribution and characteristics of power-generating facilities and then add information from a spatial dataset describing atmospheric sulfate (xSO4) deposition.

  • SO4 wet deposition - We will be adding the ESRI rest files associated with SO4 deposition to look at the occurrence of acid rain.  
    • Here is the ESRI Rest link from the website above that will provide raster files for SO4 deposition - DMS/depot_xSO4_5YA_deposition (MapServer) 
  • Power_Plants.csv
    • This dataset provides information about 

First, I want you to explore the power plants dataset and take a look at the following questions. 

  • How many of each power plant are there? 
  • How many megawatts are contributed by each power plant type? 

Provincial Water Quality Monitoring Network

Your goal for today is to conduct an exploratory data analysis on the PWQMN. You will exploring the following releases to water (Water Releases - Total). 

  • Phosphorus (total)
    • Phosphates are primarily responsible for eutrophication
  • Chloride (CHLORIDE,  UNFIL.REAC)
    • Chloride is released from road salts in the winter and has a number of adverse consequences for aquatic ecosystems.

Datasets

  • Provincial water quality monitoring network
    • Link the Provincial Water Quality Monitoring Network. Access the data you'll need. Work to get the data you want to work with. 
    • Take a collection of measurements from the PWQMN over time
      • Data 2025
      • Data 2019 - March 2021
      • Data 2000-2009
  • Conservation Authority Administrative Areas 
    • As conservation authorities help monitor and manage water quality, it would be helpful to assess water quality at the authority level boundaries
  • Ontario Roads Network
    • This dataset is useful when you are exploring the  chloride concentrations as road salt is the main cause of increased chloride concentrations
    • When using this dataset, which is very large, you should do something called creating a spatial index. To do so, just go to the geoprocessing toolbox and search for Create Spatial Index
    • You can use the Sum line lengths in the processing toolbox to calculate the total number of roads within a buffer zone
  • Ontario Watershed Boundaries (OWB) | Ontario GeoHub
    • You can download different watershed boundaries here to show determine the water quality of each watershed
Characterizing the network

Begin by characterizing the Provincial Water Quality Monitoring Network as a whole. Your goal is to understand how the program is structured, where monitoring occurs, and how sampling effort is distributed.

Use the available PWQMN datasets to build a clear picture of the monitoring program and the potential gaps in the dataset. 

  • How many monitoring stations are represented in the dataset?

  • How is sampling distributed among stations (e.g., are some stations sampled much more frequently than others?)

  • How has monitoring effort changed through time?

  • What water-quality parameters are measured most frequently?

  • Where are monitoring stations located, and are there obvious geographic concentrations or gaps?

Phosphates and chloride

Phosphates are released into the water from agricultural run-off and wastewater. Chloride occurs naturally in freshwater, but concentrations can also be influenced by human activities, including the use of road salt. Use the PWQMN data to investigate patterns in phosphate and chloride concentrations across the monitoring network.

  • How are phosphate/chloride concentrations distributed across the dataset?

  • Do concentrations differ substantially among monitoring stations?

  • How have phosphate/chloride concentrations changed through time?

  • Are there seasonal patterns in phosphate/chloride concentrations?

  • Are there particular stations or periods with unusually high concentrations?

  • Are the patterns you observe consistent across the monitoring network, or are they concentrated in particular locations?

  • How far is each monitoring station from the nearest major road or agricultural area?

  • Are stations with relatively high phosphate/chloride concentrations located closer to roads or agricultural sites ?

Exam practice

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

data1 <- read_csv("1km_buffer.csv") |> 
  clean_names()|>
  mutate(buffer = "1 km")

data2 <- read_csv("2km_buffer.csv") |> 
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(buffer = "2 km")

combined_data <- bind_rows(data1, data2) |> 
  mutate(month = month(event_date_standard, label = TRUE))

count_data <- combined_data |> 
  group_by(month, buffer) |> 
  summarize(sightings = n()) |> 
  filter(month %in% c("Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov"))

ggplot(count_data, aes(x = month, y= sightings, fill = buffer)) +
  geom_col(colour = "black")+
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Sightings", fill = "Distance from ferry route", title = "Sightings within 1 km and 2 km of the ferry", subtitle = "OBIS data from 1900-2024")+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Practice Set #2 - Crab counts 

Datasets:

  • Information_stations.csv
    • Contains information on all of the stations and tows, including the distance that each tow was run for (dist)
  • Nombre_crabe_crab_number.csv
    • Numbers of crabs (n_tot) for each tow is listed in every row with stations (st) and  years (an); however, the length of the tow is not accounted for in the total number of crabs counted, so tows that run for longer distances could have more crabs because they covered a greater area. This needs to be fixed!

Practice Exam question

Please recreate the following figure using R:

crab_counts.png

Note: For any left_joins required for this question you do not need to explicitly write which columns you want the data to be joined by as we have previously done in our join examples ("by = join_by(collection_site == station"). You can simply tell it which datasets you want to be joined and it will attach the columns by default. Example below on how you can join two datasets without specifying the join columns (pwqmn_data_2024 and unique_stations). 

pwqmn_data_2024_joined  <- pwqmn_data_2024 |>
       left_join(unique_stations)

<section id="working-through-the-activities" class="level2">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="working-through-the-activities">Working through the activities</h2>
<p>Activities use a software–section–question code: E for Excel, Q for QGIS, R for R. For example, E.1.1 is the first Excel question in case study 1. Numbering restarts for each software within each case study. For R questions, go through it in your own R script.</p>

<section id="case-study-1-north-atlantic-right-whale" class="level1">
<h1>Case study 1: North Atlantic Right Whale</h1>
<section id="files-you-need" class="level2">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="files-you-need">Files you need</h2>
<ul>
<li><code>OBIS - North Atlantic Right Whale reduced.csv</code></li>
<li>Vessel route shapefile</li>
</ul>
</section>
<section id="excel" class="level2 software-excel">
<h2 class="software-excel anchored" data-anchor-id="excel">Excel</h2>
<section id="e.1.1" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="e.1.1">E.1.1</h3>
<p>Import the CSV using Power Query (use Transform) and inspect the complete dataset. Locate the following information within the dataset:</p>
<ul>
<li>coordinates</li>
<li>dates</li>
<li>years</li>
<li>whale counts (what are they listed as?)</li>
</ul>
<ol type="a">
<li><p>The eventDate column has a range of dates. Try to parse out as many dates as you can from the column.</p></li>
<li><p>We want to examine seasonal aspects of the sightings, so create new column that provides the month (use the eventDate_standard column for this)</p></li>
<li><p>Null values in the <code>individualCount</code> column represent sightings where a whale was seen, but the number of whales was not recorded. Let’s make an assumption that these values were just a single whale and correct the data accordingly.</p></li>
<li><p>Once you exit the PowerQuery editor, make sure you save your adjusted dataset as a new csv <code>OBIS - North Atlantic Right Whale updated.csv</code></p></li>
</ol>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-1-contents" aria-controls="callout-1" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">
<div class="callout-icon-container">
<i class="callout-icon"></i>
</div>
<div class="callout-title-container flex-fill">
<span class="screen-reader-only">Tip</span>Get help
</div>
<div class="callout-btn-toggle d-inline-block border-0 py-1 ps-1 pe-0 float-end"><i class="callout-toggle"></i></div>
</div>
<div id="callout-1" class="callout-1-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>Use Data → From Text/CSV → Transform Data.</li>
<li>In Power Query, profile the entire dataset and check they key column types for any missing values.</li>
<li>Add column in the Power Query editor and select the eventDate_standard</li>
<li>Convert through the null values within the <code>individualCount</code> column to a value of 1 using either the replace values option in PowerQuery or within the table, selecting blanks and flashfilling the number 1 down the column</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="e.1.2" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="e.1.2">E.1.2</h3>
<p>The bathymetry column has the estimated depth of the whale sightings for that row. However, some bathymetry values appear to be on land (i.e. they have negative values). Create a new bathymetry column called “corrected_depth” and set all the negative values to be 0.</p>
<ol type="a">
<li>Try this via the column filter</li>
<li>Try using an if function.</li>
</ol>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-2-contents" aria-controls="callout-2" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">
<div class="callout-icon-container">
<i class="callout-icon"></i>
</div>
<div class="callout-title-container flex-fill">
<span class="screen-reader-only">Tip</span>Get help
</div>
<div class="callout-btn-toggle d-inline-block border-0 py-1 ps-1 pe-0 float-end"><i class="callout-toggle"></i></div>
</div>
<div id="callout-2" class="callout-2-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>You can initially use the column filter to select any values below zero and then replace then with 0 using a flashfill</li>
<li>To use an IF statement, you want <code>=IF([@bathymetry] <0, 0,[@bathymetry])</code>. Within Excel, we technically only used character strings, but you might have recognized that when we were using IF statements within R you can have the “FALSE” part of the IF statement just be the results in the column. So, the IF statement above reads “If the values are less than 0, then replace those values with 0, otherwise, just use the value that is already listed in the bathymetry column”</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="e.1.3" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="e.1.3">E.1.3</h3>
<ol type="a">
<li>Create a PivotTable showing the <em>number of sighting records</em> (not total sightings) by <code>institutioncode</code>. How many records have no institution recorded?</li>
<li>Sort the data by the institutions that have the highest number of sightings</li>
<li>Remove the sightings that have no institution recorded and drop any institutions that have fewer than 10 sightings recorded</li>
<li>Create a PivotChart to show how the institutions vary in their number of sightings</li>
</ol>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-3-contents" aria-controls="callout-3" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">
<div class="callout-icon-container">
<i class="callout-icon"></i>
</div>
<div class="callout-title-container flex-fill">
<span class="screen-reader-only">Tip</span>Get help
</div>
<div class="callout-btn-toggle d-inline-block border-0 py-1 ps-1 pe-0 float-end"><i class="callout-toggle"></i></div>
</div>
<div id="callout-3" class="callout-3-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>Insert a PivotTable from the cleaned table. Make sure that the entire table is selected when you create your PivotTable (selecting cell A1 will do this for you).</li>
<li>Put institution into the rows and then also put it into the values section (it should by default select count for you)</li>
<li>Use the drop-down filter to remove the rows that have no institution recorded</li>
<li>Use the same filter, using either the tick boxes to remove those institutions that have low sightings or use the value filters to remove anything less than 10</li>
<li>Insert a PivotChart</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="e.1.4" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="e.1.4">E.1.4</h3>
<ol type="a">
<li>Create a second PivotTable showing the sum of <code>individualCount</code> in each year.</li>
<li>Change the pivot chart to look at the number of sightings in each year.</li>
</ol>
<p>Do the two summaries show the same pattern? Think about what the differences are between what they measure.</p>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-4-contents" aria-controls="callout-4" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">
<div class="callout-icon-container">
<i class="callout-icon"></i>
</div>
<div class="callout-title-container flex-fill">
<span class="screen-reader-only">Tip</span>Get help
</div>
<div class="callout-btn-toggle d-inline-block border-0 py-1 ps-1 pe-0 float-end"><i class="callout-toggle"></i></div>
</div>
<div id="callout-4" class="callout-4-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>Put <code>year</code> in Rows and <code>individualCount</code> in values</li>
<li>Set value field to Sum</li>
<li>Switch the value field to look at count instead of sum</li>
<li>Compare the two pivot charts and examine the similarities and differences between them</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="e.1.5" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="e.1.5">E.1.5</h3>
<p>Create a PivotTable showing the number of total number of sightings observed by calendar month, pooled across years. Which months have the most records, and how could observation effort affect this pattern?</p>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-5-contents" aria-controls="callout-5" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">
<div class="callout-icon-container">
<i class="callout-icon"></i>
</div>
<div class="callout-title-container flex-fill">
<span class="screen-reader-only">Tip</span>Get help
</div>
<div class="callout-btn-toggle d-inline-block border-0 py-1 ps-1 pe-0 float-end"><i class="callout-toggle"></i></div>
</div>
<div id="callout-5" class="callout-5-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>Put <code>month</code> in Rows and Count of id in Values.</li>
<li>Sort months numerically from 1 to 12</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="e.1.6" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="e.1.6">E.1.6</h3>
<p>Create a PivotChart that shows the total number of sightings in the following three categories: - 1 whale seen - 2-10 whales seen - More than 10 whales seen</p>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-6-contents" aria-controls="callout-6" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">
<div class="callout-icon-container">
<i class="callout-icon"></i>
</div>
<div class="callout-title-container flex-fill">
<span class="screen-reader-only">Tip</span>Get help
</div>
<div class="callout-btn-toggle d-inline-block border-0 py-1 ps-1 pe-0 float-end"><i class="callout-toggle"></i></div>
</div>
<div id="callout-6" class="callout-6-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>You want to create a new column that creates three new categorical variables</li>
<li>The easiest approach here is to use an IFS statement</li>
<li><code>=IFS([@individualCount]>10, "More than 10", [@individualCount]> 1, "Between 2 and 10", [@individualCount] =1, "Only 1")</code></li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="e.1.7" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="e.1.7">E.1.7</h3>
<p>Create a dropdown box to select institutions and then populate a cell with the number of sightings when an institution is selected from the dropdown box.</p>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-7-contents" aria-controls="callout-7" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">
<div class="callout-icon-container">
<i class="callout-icon"></i>
</div>
<div class="callout-title-container flex-fill">
<span class="screen-reader-only">Tip</span>Get help
</div>
<div class="callout-btn-toggle d-inline-block border-0 py-1 ps-1 pe-0 float-end"><i class="callout-toggle"></i></div>
</div>
<div id="callout-7" class="callout-7-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>For this question, you want to get the unique names of each institution using the <code>UNIQUE</code> function in Excel. I would recommend doing this on a separarte sheet.</li>
<li>Then you need to create a cell that has data validation using the list of the unique vales</li>
<li>Then you want a cell that uses COUNTIF with an institution from the dropdown box as the criteria.</li>
<li>You can review the steps needed to complete this task in this video - https://westernu.brightspace.com/d2l/wcs/mp/mediaplayer.d2l?ou=198357&entryId=b068f205-e763-447f-97ee-b96d261ac420%2flatest&type=video&d2lrnc=acm52l7contentca-central-13ZwHpDhD8NbH9dCF5qzbbyvideo5mSBNOmYiGiTtjhKuCyEwM%252flatest</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="qgis" class="level2 software-qgis">
<h2 class="software-qgis anchored" data-anchor-id="qgis">QGIS</h2>
<section id="q.1.1" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="q.1.1">Q.1.1</h3>
<ol type="a">
<li><p>Load the <code>OBIS - North Atlantic Right Whale updated.csv</code>as a point layer (the one that has months in it now from above) using with WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) as the source CRS. Add the ocean basemap and inspect the sighting locations and attributes.</p></li>
<li><p>Identify any records that are showing as having a bathymetry less than 0. Explore the map where these sightings have been located. Clear the filter once you have done that.</p></li>
<li><p>Use the symbology to identify points that have bathymetry below zero and and those that have a bathymetry above zero.</p></li>
</ol>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-8-contents" aria-controls="callout-8" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">
<div class="callout-icon-container">
<i class="callout-icon"></i>
</div>
<div class="callout-title-container flex-fill">
<span class="screen-reader-only">Tip</span>Get help
</div>
<div class="callout-btn-toggle d-inline-block border-0 py-1 ps-1 pe-0 float-end"><i class="callout-toggle"></i></div>
</div>
<div id="callout-8" class="callout-8-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>Add Delimited Text Layer using longitude as X and latitude as Y.</li>
<li>Assign EPSG:4326 to the supplied geographic coordinates.</li>
<li>Add a basemap using QMS and inspect the locations.</li>
<li>Use a filter to initially find points that are recorded as being on land, then clear the filter</li>
<li>Use the field calculator to create a new text column (you must change the Output field type). Use an IF statement to create the new column - <code>IF( "bathymetry" <0, 'On land', 'On Water')</code></li>
<li>QGIS video - https://westernu.brightspace.com/d2l/wcs/mp/mediaplayer.d2l?ou=198357&entryId=a90949ef-8dd2-4096-be6a-cb03f670b0bb%2flatest&type=video&d2lrnc=acm52l7contentca-central-13ZwHpDhD8NbH9dCF5qzbbyvideo58XWN6MRLM6HNOzsVeKXcn%252flatest</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="q.1.2" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="q.1.2">Q.1.2</h3>
<ol type="a">
<li>Load the vessel route layers for:</li>
</ol>
<ul>
<li><code>TSSLPT_A.shp</code> (traffic separation lanes)</li>
<li><code>TSEZNE_A.shp</code> (area seperating the traffic separation lanes)</li>
</ul>
<p>Zoom in on the Bay of Fundy (where most of the whale sightings are). The traffic separation lanes are the pathways that vessels take to avoid each other and the area separating the traffic separation lanes is a buffer between those vessel lanes.</p>
<ol start="2" type="a">
<li><p>Create a single vector layer that contains bother the traffic separation lanes and the buffer zone between them (you can ignore any errors about field length)</p></li>
<li><p>Select the routes in the Bay of Fundy study area picture below and then save those features as a separate layer.</p></li>
</ol>
<p><img role="img" src="data:image/png;base64," class="img-fluid" width="465"></p>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-9-contents" aria-controls="callout-9" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">

<i class="callout-icon"></i>

<div class="callout-title-container flex-fill">

</div>

</div>
<div id="callout-9" class="callout-9-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>Load the vessel routes listed by dragging and dropping them into the map canvas</li>
<li>Merge the two polygon layers by going to Vector → Data Management Tools → Merge Vector layers</li>
<li>Select or filter Bay of Fundy routes by selecting the features using the select features button in QGIS. You can drag a box around all the features or alternatively use control to select all of the polygons in the Bay of Fundy you want to merge.</li>
<li>Save selected routes as a geopackage or shapefile by right-clicking on Export - Save Selected Features as. Make sure you use the three dots!</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="q.1.3" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="q.1.3">Q.1.3</h3>
<ol type="a">
<li>Change the symbology of the whale sightings to represent the month of each sighting. Style the vessel routes so they remain visible beneath the points.</li>
<li>Change the symbology on the vector layers to show the total number of sightings within each poloygon feature to identify areas where there is high potential for ship strike.<br>
</li>
<li>Create count layers that have counts for different May and August to see if there are any monthly patterns in where ship strike is likely to occur.</li>
</ol>
<div class="callout callout-style-default callout-tip callout-titled" title="Get help">
<div class="callout-header d-flex align-content-center collapsed" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target=".callout-10-contents" aria-controls="callout-10" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Toggle callout">

<div id="callout-10" class="callout-10-contents callout-collapse collapse">
<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>Open Layer Properties → Symbology → Categorized and classify sighting points using month.</li>
<li>You must use Count Points in Polygon to determine how many points are within the polygon layers that you merged in the previous question</li>
<li>Filter the original points data for the two different months and re-run the count points in poloygon feature</li>
<li>You can flash between the two layers you’ve created, but be mindful of the differences in the the symbology classifications</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="q.1.4" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="q.1.4">Q.1.4</h3>
<p>Even if some sightings don’t overlap with the vessel routes, they may be quite close to them. Calculate the distance between each point and the nearest vessel route (NAD83 / UTM zone 20N — EPSG:26920). What does a distance of zero mean?</p>

<div class="callout-body-container callout-body">
<ul>
<li>Reproject both working layers to a suitable projected CRS with metre units - NAD83 / UTM zone 20N — EPSG:26920</li>
<li>Run Join attributes by nearest with sightings first, routes second.</li>
</ul>

</div>
</div>

<section id="q.1.5" class="level3">
<h3 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="q.1.5">Q.1.5</h3>
<p>Use Field Calculator to create a distance field in kilometres. Filter the result to sightings within 5 km of a mapped route and record how many sighting records meet this condition. Then change the point symbology to represent distance from the nearest route.</p>
<p>Explain what proximity to a mapped route can tell you, and why it does not establish that a vessel was present when a whale was sighted.</p>

topics.title: Selecting a project topic and collecting data
topics.path: Assessments > Independent Project
topics.html:
Independent Project

The major project for this course is an independent data analysis assignment where you'll explore a topic of your choice. This project is intentionally open-ended, offering you the flexibility to define a reasonable scope, source relevant datasets, and conduct meaningful analyses.  It challenges you to thoughtfully plan and execute your data exploration from start to finish. A defining aspect of this project is the sourcing of data from open-source databases and repositories.

You'll take the lead in combining and analyzing datasets to uncover meaningful relationships and answer the key questions you've identified for your project.

Selecting a project topic

Based on your interests and career ambitions, you need to select a broad topic related to ecosystem health and it will be your responsibility to answer questions around the topic using temporal and spatial environmental data.  As you are highly dependent upon the data available, I would strongly recommend that you identify a general, high-level topic first and then search for datasets available around that topic. You should avoid clearly identifying a set of research questions for your analysis before first ensuring that are enough available datasets to support that project topic.  Here are a few examples of topics students have chosen in the past:

  • Southwestern Ontario: Ecosystem Health in the Presence of Neonicotinoids

  • Analyzing Air Quality near Emitting Facilities in Ontario

  • The Impact of Fossil Fuel Energy for Electricity Generation on Ecosystem Health

Critically, I think it is of utmost importance to choose a topic that resonates with you and aligns with your goals for this course and program, as well as your co-op interests. Many students have referenced their Independent projects in interviews or even shared their projects with potential employers. 

How many datasets do I need to find?

Alright, one of the most challenging and frustrating components of this project is trying to find data for your topic.  Each of you will have a specific topic. In some cases, information on that topic is compiled into large complex datasets whereas in other cases, the data may be spread out amongst several different ones. Therefore, there is no single correct answer for how many datasets each of you should find.  In your initial data exploration phase, you should attempt to find as many relevant datasets as you can in the beginning and then whittle things down to more refined questions once you understand what is available. 

Potential Data Sources

The majority of your project data will be downloaded from open-source data repositories. I've provided an initial list for your to search from below. However, in some cases you may want to craft your own datasets from other sources that are not collated in online repositories. 

Canadian Open Data Portal https://open.canada.ca/en/open-data
Ontario Open Data Portal https://data.ontario.ca/
London (Ontario) Open Data Portal https://opendata.london.ca/
World Bank Open Data https://data.worldbank.org/
Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS) https://obis.org/
iNaturalist (citizen science website) https://www.inaturalist.org/
Dryad (academic research repository) https://datadryad.org/stash
United Nations Data https://data.un.org/
eBird  https://ebird.org/home
Geoscholars portal Scholars GeoPortal

topics.html:
Final Submission

I've copied instructions for the Independent Project from the course outline and put them below. To assist with your final submission, I've added some additional information that is highlighted below in red. These updates include:

  • A word limit for the written summary (2000 words)
  • Clarification on the infographic
  • Clarification on interactive maps

I've now uploaded a Rubric for the final submission, which you can view by clicking on the Independent Project assignment under the Assignments Tab - Independent Project (30%)

Due Date: December 11th, 11:59 PM

StoryMap Examples

I've pulled an example posted by SFU, but please note that this is not aligned with our StoryMap structure (e.g., they have an Intro, Methods, Results, Discussion section) and does not include the same emphasis on the visualizations that is required for our course.  I've also included a link below to the ArcGIS StoryMap project gallery. These are not templates for your own StoryMap, but merely some examples to possibly get inspiration from.

You are welcome to include photos in your StoryMap to enhance the clarity and visual appeal of your work. These may support the StoryMap component of your grade (7 of 60 points); however, please ensure that your primary focus is on clearly communicating your findings from your data analysis.

  • Watershed Ecology
  • Project Gallery 

Project description (copied from course outline)

The final deliverable for your project is a comprehensive ArcGIS storymap that highlights the results of your analysis and provides interpretation by effectively integrating text, figures, maps, and tables into one flowing document. We have scheduled an elective ArcGIS storymaps and dashboards workshop for you on November 6th and unless you feel very confident using storymaps and dashboards
already, I would strongly recommend that you attend that workshop. Storymaps are a fun and interactive way to share data visualizations (we’ll review examples throughout the course) and this project will give you (1) practice on how to best use storymaps and dashboards and (2) a final deliverable you can share with potential co-op employers

  •  Infographic - You will create a `social media ready` infographic that provides an overview and summary of your analysis for the public. You can prepare this infographic in something like PowerPoint or Canva and then include it as a picture within your overall StoryMap.  Your infographic should be something engaging that conveys the main, high-level findings of your project (i.e. it does not need to include all of your findings).

    • I've provided some examples from previous infographics below. Please note, if you use figures or maps in your infographic, please make sure they are readable in your infographic (e.g., increase the font size relative to the figure size).
      • Bird_infographic.png
      • Climate infographic.png
      • august complex infographic.pdf

  •  Figures – You will need 10 figures created using R

  • Maps - 10 maps created in QGIS (with at least two interactive maps). For your interactive maps, you will be using spatial data you processed within QGIS, but are just displaying it in an interactive format within StoryMaps (i.e. not a static image). Your dashboard can count towards one of your interactive maps. 

  • Dashboard - at least one dashboard created within your ArcGIS StoryMap

  • Written summary - A written interpretation to go along with your data visualizations and analysis that summarizes your key findings. Make sure to cite all figures and maps that you include. While interpreting your results be sure to incorporate references from academic literature to provide context; however, the emphasis should be primarily on your analysis and interpretation of the open-source data you have gathered. Your written summary should not exceed 2000 words. 

  • A list of data sources - Provide a list of data sources you used for your project with weblinks to each of them.

  • References section - include any academic references you have cited in your assignment. Use APA 7th edition for your reference format.

    All figures, graphs, or maps should be created (by you) from data you have collected from various open sources.

National Pollutant Release Inventory  Report

Background

Our class will be collaborating with Environment and Climate Change Canada on data analysis for the National Pollutant Release Inventory (NPRI).  ECCC has provided us with some key target areas they would like more information on and you and your team will be conducting an exploratory data analysis using the NPRI dataset.

Project objectives

How comparable are the Canadian and German reporting datasets, and what can they tell us about differences in reported industrial releases to air?

Your project has two sections. First, assess the comparability of the reporting systems across releases to air and disposals or waste transfers (this is what Carlos was stressing in his presentation). Then use that assessment to prepare a comparable air-release dataset and investigate differences between countries and industrial sectors.

Section 1: Assess dataset comparability

Compare the Canadian National Pollutant Release Inventory (NPRI) and German pollutant release and transfer data. Your assessment should consider both releases to air and disposals or waste transfers, using the categories available in each reporting system.

Develop a comparison addressing the following:

  • How do reporting thresholds and requirements vary by substance, activity, or reporting category? Which facilities or quantities might be excluded? 
  • The German data includes threshold data in the CSV. You can find Canadian threshold data here - 

    Canadian NPRI substance list and thresholds

  • How many substances or substance groups are covered by each program? Where is their overlap between the two programs? 
  • How are the reporting methodologies reported (e.g.,  measured, calculated, or estimated in the German data) and how does this differ between the programs?
  • What units are used and what conversions would be necessary? Are there some substances that cannot be converted?
  • Do the datasets cover matching periods and equivalent industrial activities? Briefly consider whether the NACE and NAICS categories in the sector table describe comparable activities.

Explain which comparisons are defensible, which require standardization, and which cannot be made reliably. Support your assessment with reporting documentation and examples from the datasets.

Section 2: Build and analyse a comparable air-release dataset

Use your assessment to construct a combined dataset for comparing releases to air from your selected industrial sectors in Canada and Germany.

Document your decisions about:

  • The years, sectors, and substances retained.
  • How substance names and sector classifications were matched.
  • Unit conversions and other transformations.
  • How reporting thresholds, missing values, and unmatched records were handled.
  • Any remaining differences that standardization cannot resolve.

Use the combined dataset to investigate how reported air releases vary between countries and sectors. Present clear summaries and well-chosen visualizations, and explain the main patterns.

Assignment format

As a group, prepare a report that explains your comparability assessment, dataset preparation, analysis, and conclusions. Use tables, figures, and maps where they help support your findings.

Your report should include:

  • A table of contents.
  • A short executive summary for each section (250 words each). 
  • A short introduction to the sector in section 1 (300 words max)
  • A table and supporting discussion for Section 1.
  • Relevant visualizations and maps for both sections in the report. 
  • References

Submit your standardized air-release dataset alongside the report.

Please keep your report between 30-40 pages maximum. Groups with three students may have shorter reports. 

    Past collaborations from other institutions

    Below, you can find examples of past projects. Please note that these examples are provided simply to illustrate the types of reports previously submitted to the program and are not necessarily intended as models of exemplary project work.

    • Bisphenol A and Bis(2-ethylhexyl) Adipate releases from different facilities across Canada
    • Analysis of Biphenyl and Bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate releases and exposure in diverse water bodies in Canada

    Dates and deadlines

    • Polished draft to ECCC for review  -  December 2nd, 2026, Submission portal for assignment
    • Virtual presentations to ECCC mentors - December 2nd, 2026 (in class) 
    • When feedback has been received from your ECCC mentor, you will have a set period of time to complete updates to the document before final submission. This will form part of your grade for the assignment.  

    As part of this project, I would like you to complete the MES Team Charter Template linked below and upload it to Brightspace. 

    • MES Team Charter Template .docx
